qs.q: A 58-year-old man with a massive pulmonary embolism presents with sudden cardiovascular collapse, distended neck veins, and hypotension. What specific category of shock does this clinical picture represent?
qs.e: A massive pulmonary embolism creates a mechanical obstruction to right ventricular outflow, classifying it as obstructive shock with typical elevated jugular venous pressure. Cardiogenic shock stems from primary pump failure rather than mechanical pulmonary outflow obstruction.
qs.s: Surgical Critical Care: ICU, Respiratory Failure, Ventilation, Blood: MCQs

qs.q: A 62-year-old woman undergoes a total abdominal hysterectomy. On the 2nd post-operative day, she exhibits sudden shortness of breath, pleuritic chest pain, and a heart rate of 125 beats per minute. Which diagnostic modality is considered standard for confirming pulmonary embolism in this acute setting?
qs.e: CT pulmonary angiography is a primary diagnostic test for pulmonary embolism. Plain chest radiography lacks sufficient sensitivity and specificity to confirm a pulmonary embolus.
qs.s: Post-operative Care and Complications of Surgery: MCQs

qs.q: Paradoxical embolism is a recognized complication of which cardiac abnormality?
qs.e: Paradoxical embolism occurs when a thrombus from the venous system crosses into the arterial circulation through a right-to-left shunt, such as an ASD or VSD with reversed flow. Purely obstructive lesions do not permit direct venous-to-arterial passage.

qs.q: What is the most common origin of thrombi responsible for causing a pulmonary embolism?
o: Superior vena cava forming central thrombi
Right ventricular apex forming mural thrombi
Deep leg veins forming peripheral thrombi
Pulmonary artery intima forming local thrombi
qs.e: Pulmonary embolisms are most commonly caused by thrombi originating from the deep veins of the lower extremities. Right heart or local arterial sources are much less frequent.

qs.q: A 58-man admitted for a pulmonary embolism is started on a continuous infusion of an anticoagulant that binds antithrombin III. Which laboratory test is most appropriate for therapeutic monitoring of this medication?
qs.e: Unfractionated heparin is monitored via the activated partial thromboplastin time because it primarily affects the intrinsic coagulation pathway. The international normalised ratio is instead used to monitor vitamin K antagonists like warfarin.
qs.s: Acute Leukaemia (AML/ALL) & WBC Disorders: Haematology Guide: MCQs

qs.q: A patient with pulmonary embolism presents with low blood pressure below 90 mmHg, a condition termed massive PE. What is the preferred treatment approach?
o: Thrombolytic therapy to rapidly dissolve the clot
Application of compression stockings and early ambulation
Immediate outpatient discharge with direct oral anticoagulants
Inferior vena cava filter placement without medical therapy
qs.e: Massive PE with low blood pressure requires thrombolytic therapy because standard anticoagulants will not rapidly resolve the massive clot. Outpatient management is reserved for stable, simple PE.

qs.q: Why does a pulmonary embolism frequently cause a pleural effusion?
o: Severe reduction in systemic oncotic pressure from renal protein loss
Passive transdiaphragmatic movement of peritoneal ascites into the chest
Traumatic disruption of the thoracic duct results in chylous fluid leakage
Ischemic pulmonary vascular obstruction increases pleural membrane permeability
qs.e: Vascular obstruction from a pulmonary embolism increases pleural permeability, which eventually causes a transudative or exudative effusion. Diaphragmatic defects and thoracic duct rupture account for hepatic hydrothorax and chylothorax respectively.

qs.q: A pulmonary embolism causes a pleural effusion through which primary mechanism?
o: Rupture of the thoracic duct into the pleural space
Bacterial infection spreading directly into the pleural cavity
Extensive damage to the left ventricular muscle
Obstruction causing increased pleural blood vessel permeability
qs.e: Obstruction by a pulmonary embolism increases pleural permeability, which eventually causes a transudative or exudative effusion. It does not involve direct bacterial invasion or thoracic duct rupture.

es.q: An autopsy reveals significant obstruction of the pulmonary vasculature, leading to sudden death. What percentage of the pulmonary vasculature is typically obstructed to cause sudden death in the context of a pulmonary embolism?
es.m: Sudden death due to pulmonary embolism typically occurs when more than 60% of the pulmonary vasculature is obstructed (5 marks).

es.q: A 70-year-old patient suddenly collapses and dies due to a massive pulmonary embolism. a) From which anatomical location do most pulmonary emboli commonly arise? b) What percentage of the pulmonary vasculature typically needs to be obstructed to cause sudden death in pulmonary embolism? c) Explain w
es.m: a) Most pulmonary emboli commonly arise from the **deep veins of the lower legs**. b) Sudden death typically occurs when **more than 60%** of the pulmonary vasculature is obstructed. c) Pulmonary infarction occurs in only about 10% of cases due to the **dual blood supply of the lungs**. The lungs receive blood from both the pulmonary arteries (carrying deoxygenated blood) and the bronchial arteries (carrying oxygenated systemic blood). This dual supply often provides sufficient collateral circulation to prevent tissue necrosis even if a pulmonary artery is blocked.
es.s: Respiratory System Pathology 1A — Practice Questions — Essay Questions

es.q: In the context of pulmonary embolism (PE), explain why pulmonary infarction occurs in only a minority of cases, and what degree of pulmonary vasculature obstruction is associated with sudden death.
es.m: Pulmonary infarction occurs in only about 10% of pulmonary embolism cases due to the dual blood supply of the lungs (pulmonary and bronchial arteries), providing collateral circulation. Sudden death from a pulmonary embolism typically occurs when more than 60% of the pulmonary vasculature is obstructed.

es.q: **Stroke in a young adult with PFO?** **Paradoxical embolism**.
es.m:
- **Mechanism:** A patent foramen ovale (PFO) allows blood to flow directly from the right atrium to the left atrium under certain pressure gradients.
- **Paradoxical embolism:** A venous thrombus (e.g., from deep vein thrombosis) bypasses the pulmonary circulation via the PFO and enters the arterial system.
- **Cerebral circulation:** The embolus travels up the aorta and lodges in the cerebral circulation, causing an ischemic stroke.
- **Risk demographic:** Particularly important to investigate as a cause of cryptogenic stroke in young adults without traditional cardiovascular risk factors.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: An embolism is the lodging of an embolus, a detached intravascular solid, liquid, or gaseous mass, in a blood vessel, causing obstruction. This obstruction can lead to ischemia and infarction in the affected tissue. The clinical presentation varies greatly depending on the location and size of the embolus.

sections.p: An embolus is a mobile intravascular mass that is carried by the blood to a site distant from its origin, where it lodges and obstructs blood flow. The most common type is a thromboembolism, originating from a thrombus. Diagnosis involves identifying the embolus and its impact on organ function.
b: Thromboembolism: Most common, usually from a DVT or cardiac mural thrombus.
Fat embolism: Associated with bone fractures or trauma, leading to fat globules in circulation.
Air embolism: Can occur during surgery, central line insertion, or decompression sickness.
Amniotic fluid embolism: Rare but severe complication of labor and delivery.
Tumor embolism: Fragments of malignant tumors entering the bloodstream.

sections.p: The severity of an embolism depends on the size of the embolus, the vessel it obstructs, and the collateral circulation available. For pulmonary embolism (PE), severity is often assessed by hemodynamic stability and right ventricular strain.
b: Massive PE: Hemodynamic instability (hypotension, shock).
Submassive PE: Right ventricular dysfunction or myocardial necrosis without systemic hypotension.
Low-risk PE: No markers of right ventricular dysfunction or myocardial injury.

sections.p: The most frequent cause of embolism is a thrombus, leading to a thromboembolism. These often originate in the deep veins of the legs (causing pulmonary embolism) or in the heart (causing systemic emboli).
b: Deep vein thrombosis (DVT): Primary source for pulmonary emboli.
Atrial fibrillation: Leads to stasis and clot formation in the left atrium, causing systemic emboli.
Myocardial infarction: Mural thrombi can form over infarcted ventricular walls.
Valvular heart disease: Rheumatic heart disease can cause thrombi on damaged valves.
Atherosclerotic plaques: Fragments can dislodge and embolize (atheroembolism).
Trauma/fractures: Release of fat globules into circulation (fat embolism).
Surgery/procedures: Introduction of air (air embolism).

sections.p: Clinical presentation varies widely based on the site of embolization. Pulmonary embolism often presents with sudden onset dyspnea and chest pain, while cerebral embolism can cause stroke symptoms.
b: Pulmonary embolism: Dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, cough, hemoptysis, syncope, tachycardia.
Cerebral embolism: Sudden neurological deficits (e.g., hemiparesis, aphasia), often affecting the middle cerebral artery.
Mesenteric embolism: Severe abdominal pain, often out of proportion to physical findings, nausea, vomiting.
Renal embolism: Flank pain, hematuria, acute kidney injury.
Peripheral arterial embolism: Sudden pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis (the 5 Ps).

sections.p: Investigations aim to confirm the presence of an embolus, identify its source, and assess organ damage. The choice of investigation depends on the suspected location.

t.b: Answers: Is there recent clot formation and breakdown? A negative result in a low-probability patient makes PE or DVT unlikely. A positive result is non-specific and requires further investigation.
Answers: Is there a pulmonary embolus in the pulmonary arteries? A positive result shows filling defects in the pulmonary arteries. If unavailable, a V/Q scan may be used.
Answers: Is there a deep vein thrombosis (DVT) in the legs, a common source for PE? A positive result shows non-compressibility of a vein, indicating a DVT.
Answers: Are there signs of right heart strain or other cardiac issues? May show sinus tachycardia, S1Q3T3 pattern, or right bundle branch block in PE. Not diagnostic for embolism itself.
Answers: Is there right ventricular dysfunction or a cardiac source for emboli? Can show right ventricular dilation or thrombi in the heart chambers.
Answers: Is there evidence of cerebral infarction due to embolism? Shows ischemic changes in the brain. Useful for diagnosing cerebral embolism.
Answers: Is there hypoxemia or respiratory acidosis? May show hypoxemia and respiratory alkalosis in PE, but not specific.

Answers: Is there cardiac strain, particularly right ventricular strain in PE? Elevated levels suggest cardiac stress, but can also be raised in kidney failure, atrial fibrillation, and older age, and lower in obesity.

sections.p: Red flags indicate severe or life-threatening embolism, requiring immediate intervention. Complications can include organ damage, chronic conditions, and death.
b: Sudden onset dyspnea, chest pain, or syncope (suggests massive PE).
Acute neurological deficit (suggests cerebral embolism/stroke).
Severe, unexplained abdominal pain (suggests mesenteric ischemia).
Hypotension and shock (indicates hemodynamic instability).
Development of gangrene in peripheral embolism.
Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) after PE.
Infarction and permanent organ damage.

sections.p: Management focuses on stabilizing the patient, preventing further embolization, and treating the underlying cause. Anticoagulation is central to managing thromboembolism.
b: Anticoagulation: Heparin (unfractionated or low molecular weight) or direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) to prevent clot growth and new clot formation.
Thrombolysis: Fibrinolytic drugs (e.g., alteplase) for massive PE or severe systemic emboli to dissolve the clot.
Embolectomy: Surgical or catheter-based removal of the embolus in severe cases.
IVC filter: Placement in the inferior vena cava for patients with contraindications to anticoagulation or recurrent PE despite anticoagulation.
Supportive care: Oxygen therapy, pain management, and hemodynamic support.
Target INR for provoked pulmonary embolism is 2 to 3 (aim 2.5) for at least 3 months.

sections.p: Follow-up involves monitoring for complications and adherence to treatment. Prevention focuses on addressing risk factors for embolus formation.
b: Long-term anticoagulation for unprovoked emboli or recurrent events.
Regular monitoring for post-thrombotic syndrome after DVT.
Early mobilization after surgery or prolonged bed rest.
Compression stockings for DVT prevention.
Management of underlying conditions like atrial fibrillation or heart failure.
Smoking cessation and blood pressure control to reduce atherosclerosis risk.

sections.p: Embolism can mimic other conditions, making accurate diagnosis crucial. Distinguishing features are key to appropriate management.
b: Myocardial infarction: Can present with chest pain, but ECG and cardiac biomarkers differ from PE.
Pneumonia/Pleurisy: Can cause chest pain and dyspnea, but imaging and infectious markers help differentiate from PE.
Panic attack: Symptoms like dyspnea and tachycardia can overlap with PE, but lack objective signs of embolism.
Asthma/COPD exacerbation: Wheezing and history of lung disease are more prominent, but PE can worsen these conditions.

sections.p: Certain test results can be misleading, requiring careful clinical correlation and consideration of patient factors.
b: Negative D-dimer: Can be falsely negative in small, old clots or if testing is delayed.
Normal chest X-ray in PE: A significant PE can occur with a normal chest X-ray; it is not sensitive enough to rule out PE.
BNP elevation: While elevated in PE, it's also raised in kidney failure, atrial fibrillation, and older age, and lower in obesity, so it's not specific for PE.
Pleural effusion in PE: Can be either transudate or exudate, and often blood-stained, which can complicate interpretation of effusion analysis.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden shortness of breath or difficulty breathing
Sudden, severe chest pain, especially if worse with breathing
Sudden weakness or numbness on one side of the body, or difficulty speaking
Sudden, severe pain, pallor, coldness, or loss of movement in a limb

faq.q: What is the difference between a thrombus and an embolus?
faq.a: A thrombus is a blood clot that forms and remains attached to a vessel wall. An embolus is a detached intravascular mass (often a piece of a thrombus) that travels through the bloodstream and lodges elsewhere.

faq.q: Can an embolism happen in any part of the body?
faq.a: Yes, an embolism can occur in any blood vessel in the body, depending on the origin of the embolus and the circulatory pathway it takes. Common sites include the lungs, brain, heart, kidneys, and limbs.

The severity of an embolism varies. While some can be life-threatening (e.g., massive pulmonary embolism, cerebral embolism causing stroke), others may cause less severe, but still significant, damage to organs.

exam: A 65-year-old patient presents with sudden onset dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain. Outline your initial diagnostic approach to rule out pulmonary embolism, including relevant investigations and their expected findings.
Discuss the common sources of systemic arterial emboli and explain the clinical consequences of embolization to different arterial territories.
Describe the management principles for a patient diagnosed with a large deep vein thrombosis (DVT) who is at high risk of pulmonary embolism, including both acute and long-term strategies.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: Focused history and systematic examination allow rapid identification of embolic syndromes and severity, especially where imaging is delayed.
b: Onset: sudden vs. gradual; exact time of symptom appearance.
Risk factors: recent surgery, immobilisation, long travel, pregnancy, malignancy, known DVT, atrial fibrillation, valve disease, trauma, fractures.

Symptoms by site: dyspnoea, pleuritic chest pain, cough, haemoptysis (pulmonary); focal neuro deficit, speech change (cerebral); abdominal pain out of proportion (mesenteric); flank pain, haematuria (renal); cold, pale limb, loss of pulse (peripheral).
Associated features: syncope, tachycardia, hypotension, fever, leg swelling, calf tenderness, recent central line or scuba dive.
Examination – general: assess mental status, oxygen saturation, blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate.
Cardiopulmonary exam: inspect for distress, auscultate for tachycardia, right‑sided S4, tricuspid regurgitation murmur, pleural rub, crackles; note any new right‑sided heart sounds.

Peripheral vascular exam: palpate pulses, assess capillary refill, temperature, colour; perform the 5 Ps (pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis). Positive finding = acute arterial occlusion.
Lower‑limb exam: calf tenderness, Homan’s sign (pain on dorsiflexion) – supportive but not diagnostic; look for swelling, warmth, Homans is not reliable.
Bedside tests that cannot replace imaging: a normal ECG does not exclude PE; absence of leg swelling does not rule out DVT; peripheral pulses may be present despite distal emboli.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Use a stepwise algorithm: bedside risk scores, bedside tests, then definitive imaging. When a test is unavailable, rely on clinical probability and alternative modalities.
b: Wells or revised Geneva score – quantifies pre‑test probability for PE; low (<2), intermediate (2‑6), high (>6). Guides need for D‑dimer or imaging.
D‑dimer (quantitative) – rules out PE when <0.5 µg/mL FEU in low‑risk patients; use age‑adjusted cut‑off (age × 0.01 µg/mL) in patients > 50 y.
ECG – looks for right‑heart strain (S1Q3T3, RBBB, T‑wave inversion in V1‑V4); a normal ECG does not exclude PE.
Chest X‑ray – excludes alternative diagnoses; may show Westermark sign or Hampton hump but low sensitivity.
CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) – gold standard; positive when intraluminal filling defect in pulmonary artery; assess right‑ventricular/left‑ventricular (RV/LV) diameter ratio > 1 for severity.
Ventilation‑perfusion (V/Q) scan – useful when CTPA contraindicated; high‑probability pattern = mismatched perfusion defects.
Compression ultrasonography of lower limbs – detects proximal DVT; a positive result in high‑risk PE can obviate need for CTPA.
Echocardiography (transthoracic) – bedside assessment of RV dilation, McConnell’s sign; indicates massive/sub‑massive PE when RV dysfunction present.
Laboratory: arterial blood gas – often shows PaO₂ < 80 mmHg and respiratory alkalosis; does not diagnose PE.
When CTPA unavailable: rely on high clinical probability, positive D‑dimer, bedside echo, and lower‑limb Doppler; consider empiric anticoagulation if risk outweighs bleeding.

t.b: Estimates pre‑test probability; low risk → D‑dimer, high risk → imaging directly.
Rules out PE in low‑risk patients; result < (age × 0.01) µg/mL FEU is negative.
Shows filling defect; RV/LV ratio > 1 suggests haemodynamic compromise.
High‑probability pattern (multiple segmental mismatches) supports PE when CTPA not feasible.
Detects proximal DVT; positive result in high‑risk PE can confirm source.
RV dilation, septal flattening, McConnell’s sign indicate massive/sub‑massive PE.

sections.p: Classification combines clinical risk, imaging, and haemodynamic impact to guide therapy.
b: Massive PE – sustained systolic BP < 90 mmHg, or need for vasopressors, or cardiac arrest.
Sub‑massive PE – normotensive but evidence of RV dysfunction (RV/LV > 1, troponin rise, BNP elevation).
Low‑risk PE – no RV dysfunction, normal biomarkers, stable haemodynamics.
PE severity score (PESI/ sPESI) – stratifies mortality risk; points for age, cancer, chronic cardiopulmonary disease, HR ≥ 110, SBP < 100, O₂ < 90 %.
Pulmonary infarction occurs in < 15 % of PE because dual blood supply; when infarction present, look for pleural‑based wedge‑shaped opacity.

sections.p: Several acute presentations mimic embolic events; careful history, exam and targeted tests separate them.
b: Acute coronary syndrome – chest pain, dyspnoea; ECG shows ST changes, troponin rise; coronary angiography differentiates.
Aortic dissection – tearing chest/back pain, pulse deficit; CT aortogram or trans‑esophageal echo required.
Pneumonia/pneumonitis – fever, productive cough, infiltrates on X‑ray; sputum culture, lack of RV strain.
Pericardial tamponade – hypotension, muffled heart sounds, JVD; bedside echo shows pericardial fluid, not pulmonary artery obstruction.
Septic emboli (e.g., from IV drug use) – multiple peripheral nodules, fever; blood cultures positive, imaging shows cavitary lesions.

t.b: Chest pain with ECG ST changes, troponin rise; CTPA normal, coronary angiography positive.
Sharp tearing pain, pulse asymmetry; CT aortogram shows intimal flap, not pulmonary embolus.
Fever, productive cough, lobar infiltrate; no RV dilation, normal D‑dimer.
Beck’s triad, echo shows pericardial effusion with diastolic collapse; pressures equalize, not embolic.
Fever, multiple lung nodules with cavitation; blood cultures positive, often from right‑sided endocarditis.

sections.p: Treat embolism by stabilising the patient, initiating anticoagulation, and providing definitive therapy when indicated. Escalation is guided by haemodynamic status and imaging.
b: 1. Immediate airway, breathing, circulation support – oxygen, IV access, fluid bolus if haemodynamic compromise.
2. Rapid bedside assessment for shock: pulse, BP, JVP, peripheral perfusion.
3. Start therapeutic anticoagulation with low‑molecular‑weight heparin (LMWH) or unfractionated heparin (UFH) if renal function is impaired or LMWH contraindicated.
4. If massive or submassive pulmonary embolism with RV dysfunction, consider thrombolysis with tissue‑plasminogen activator; weigh bleeding risk.
5. For isolated systemic arterial emboli, perform urgent embolectomy or catheter‑guided thrombectomy if available.
6. Monitor anticoagulation: anti‑Xa for LMWH, aPTT for UFH; adjust dose to target range.
7. Re‑assess haemodynamics every 2–4 hours; repeat bedside echocardiography if RV strain develops.
8. Escalate to intensive care or surgical referral if persistent hypotension, refractory hypoxaemia, or organ failure occurs.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Anticoagulants and thrombolytics carry bleeding risks and drug interactions that must be monitored and managed.
b: 1. LMWH: bruising, haemorrhage; monitor anti‑Xa if renal failure or obesity; avoid in severe thrombocytopenia.
2. UFH: variable response, heparin‑induced thrombocytopenia; monitor aPTT, check platelets daily.
3. Vitamin K antagonists: warfarin – INR monitoring every 1–3 days until stable; avoid NSAIDs, antibiotics that alter gut flora.
4. Thrombolytics: major bleeding, intracranial haemorrhage; stop immediately if bleeding occurs, give protamine for UFH reversal.
5. Antiplatelet agents: increase bleeding risk when combined with anticoagulants; review necessity before adding aspirin or clopidogrel.
6. Herbal remedies (e.g., ginkgo, garlic): potentiate anticoagulation; advise discontinuation 2 weeks before surgery or thrombolysis.
7. Alcohol: increases bleeding risk; counsel abstinence during treatment period.

sections.p: Complications arise from both the embolus and its treatment; early recognition dictates escalation.
b: 1. Recurrent embolism – repeat imaging if new symptoms; consider catheter‑guided thrombectomy.
2. Haemorrhagic transformation – any drop in haemoglobin, overt bleeding; stop anticoagulation, give blood products.
3. Pulmonary hypertension – persistent RV strain; refer for advanced pulmonary hypertension management.
4. Organ infarction (renal, mesenteric) – abdominal pain, rising lactate; urgent surgical evaluation.
5. Deep vein thrombosis progression – swelling, pain; consider mechanical prophylaxis if anticoagulation contraindicated.
6. Anticoagulant‑induced skin necrosis – purple lesions; discontinue drug, switch to alternative anticoagulant.
7. Thrombolysis failure – persistent hypoxaemia; consider rescue surgery or ECMO in tertiary centres.

sections.p: Co‑morbidities and medications modify presentation, diagnostics and therapy.
b: 1. HIV – increased thrombotic risk; monitor for drug interactions with antiretrovirals; consider LMWH over warfarin.
2. TB – chronic inflammation, potential for drug‑drug interactions with rifampicin; adjust anticoagulant dose.
3. Malnutrition – low protein, impaired coagulation; avoid high‑dose vitamin K antagonists.
4. Pregnancy – use LMWH (unfractionated if renal failure); avoid warfarin due to teratogenicity.
5. Diabetes – higher risk of vascular disease; monitor for bleeding due to microvascular changes.
6. Herbal remedies – garlic, ginkgo, St. John’s wort; counsel cessation before anticoagulation.
7. Alcohol – chronic use increases bleeding risk; advise abstinence.
8. Renal failure – LMWH accumulation; use UFH or dose‑adjusted LMWH; monitor anti‑Xa closely.
9. Liver failure – impaired synthesis of clotting factors; avoid warfarin, use UFH with aPTT monitoring.
10. Age extremes – elderly: higher bleeding risk, use lower LMWH doses; children: weight‑based dosing, monitor anti‑Xa.

sections.p: Tailored approaches are required for children, pregnancy, elderly, HIV patients, and low‑resource settings.
b: 1. Children – weight‑based LMWH dosing; monitor anti‑Xa; avoid warfarin due to variable metabolism.
2. Pregnancy – LMWH preferred; monitor anti‑Xa; avoid warfarin and thrombolytics unless life‑threatening.
3. Elderly – start with lower LMWH dose, monitor anti‑Xa; consider renal function; avoid high‑dose warfarin.
4. HIV patients – monitor drug interactions with protease inhibitors; use LMWH; monitor anti‑Xa; consider therapeutic drug monitoring for warfarin.
5. Low‑resource settings – use LMWH if anti‑Xa testing unavailable; rely on clinical scoring (Wells, Geneva); consider low‑dose UFH with aPTT; use bedside echocardiography for RV strain.

sections.p: Sample questions to test comprehensive knowledge of embolism management.
b: 1. A 70‑year‑old with sudden dyspnoea and hypotension – what type of shock is this and what is the first line treatment?
2. A patient on warfarin develops a sudden headache – what is the most likely complication and how do you manage it?
3. In a patient with renal failure (CrCl 20 mL/min) who needs anticoagulation for PE, which agent is preferred and why?
4. A pregnant woman with a massive PE – which anticoagulant is safest and what monitoring is required?
5. A patient on LMWH develops a bruised area – what laboratory test would you order and what is the next step?
6. A 55‑year‑old man with HIV on protease inhibitors presents with a new embolus – how does the antiretroviral therapy affect anticoagulation choice?
7. A child with a sudden limb pain after a fracture – what type of embolism is suspected and what initial test would you order?
8. A patient with a history of TB and current PE – how might rifampicin affect warfarin therapy?
9. A patient with a massive PE and a history of bleeding – what alternative therapy can be considered?
10. A patient with a paradoxical embolus – what cardiac defect is most likely responsible?

facts: D-dimer <0.5 µg/mL FEU rules out PE; age‑adjusted cut‑off = age × 0.01 µg/mL FEU for patients >50 years.
PaO₂ <80 mmHg and respiratory alkalosis are typical ABG findings in PE; no fixed A‑a gradient threshold.
Low‑molecular‑weight heparin (LMWH) is preferred in low‑resource settings; reduced dosing is acceptable for CrCl 15–30 mL/min with monitoring.
INR is checked every 1–3 days after starting VKAs until stable; then less frequently.
Unfractionated heparin (UFH) is used when anti‑Xa monitoring is unavailable; aPTT target 1.5–2.5× control.
Pulmonary infarction is uncommon; sudden death usually requires >50–60 % of pulmonary arterial tree occluded.
Air embolism causing cardiovascular collapse typically involves >0.5 mL/kg of air; exact volume varies.
Sub‑therapeutic aPTT (1.2× control) requires increasing UFH dose, not maintaining it.

vivas.q: What is the most common source of a pulmonary embolus?
vivas.a: Deep vein thrombosis in the lower limbs.

vivas.q: A 65‑year‑old presents with sudden dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain. What is the first bedside test you would perform?
vivas.a: Check for tachycardia, hypotension, and use a bedside ultrasound to look for right ventricular strain or deep vein thrombosis.

vivas.q: Why is a D‑dimer test useful in suspected PE?
vivas.a: It is highly sensitive; a negative result in a low‑risk patient effectively rules out PE.

vivas.q: Explain the difference between massive, submassive and low‑risk PE.
vivas.a: Massive PE causes hypotension; submassive has RV dysfunction without hypotension; low‑risk has no RV dysfunction or myocardial injury.

vivas.q: What is the preferred initial anticoagulant in a patient with renal impairment (CrCl 20 mL/min) and suspected PE?
vivas.a: LMWH at a reduced dose, monitoring anti‑Xa if available; UFH is an alternative if anti‑Xa not available.

vivas.q: A patient with PE has a PaO₂ of 70 mmHg and a PaCO₂ of 30 mmHg. What does this indicate?
vivas.a: Hypoxemia with respiratory alkalosis, typical of PE.

vivas.q: Why is a pleural effusion common in PE?
vivas.a: It is a reactive exudate due to inflammation and increased vascular permeability.

vivas.q: What is paradoxical embolism and which cardiac defect predisposes to it?
vivas.a: An embolus passes from venous to arterial system via a right‑to‑left shunt; a patent foramen ovale (PFO) or atrial septal defect (ASD) is common.

vivas.q: A 58‑year‑old man with massive PE is hypotensive. What is the first-line treatment?
vivas.a: Thrombolysis with tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) if no contraindication; otherwise consider surgical embolectomy.

vivas.q: Which laboratory test is used to monitor therapeutic LMWH?
vivas.a: Anti‑Xa activity; target 0.3–0.7 IU/mL for therapeutic range.

vivas.q: What is the typical threshold for a positive D‑dimer in a 70‑year‑old?
Why is a low‑molecular‑weight heparin preferred over UFH in low‑resource settings?
vivas.a: Predictable pharmacokinetics, no need for aPTT monitoring, and lower risk of heparin‑induced thrombocytopenia.

vivas.q: Explain why pulmonary infarction occurs in only a minority of PE cases.
vivas.a: Collateral circulation and variable embolus size mean that complete occlusion of a segmental artery is required for infarction.

vivas.q: A patient with PE has an INR of 1.2 after starting warfarin. What should you do?
vivas.a: Increase the warfarin dose; do not maintain the current dose.

mcqs.q: A 62‑year‑old woman develops sudden dyspnea 2 days after hysterectomy. Which imaging is most appropriate?
mcqs.e: CT pulmonary angiography is the gold standard for acute PE.

mcqs.q: A patient with PE is started on LMWH. Which lab should you monitor if anti‑Xa is available?
Which of the following is a contraindication to thrombolysis in PE?
mcqs.e: Recent intracranial hemorrhage is a major contraindication.

cases.v: A 55‑year‑old man presents with sudden onset shortness of breath, pleuritic chest pain, and tachycardia. He has a history of recent knee replacement.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
What bedside test would you perform first?
qs.a: Check for signs of DVT in the legs and perform a focused cardiac ultrasound for RV strain.

exam: What is the most common source of a pulmonary embolus? — Deep vein thrombosis in the lower limbs.

A 65‑year‑old presents with sudden dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain. What is the first bedside test you would perform? — Check for tachycardia, hypotension, and use a bedside ultrasound to look for right ventricular strain or deep vein thrombosis.
Why is a D‑dimer test useful in suspected PE? — It is highly sensitive; a negative result in a low‑risk patient effectively rules out PE.

Explain the difference between massive, submassive and low‑risk PE. — Massive PE causes hypotension; submassive has RV dysfunction without hypotension; low‑risk has no RV dysfunction or myocardial injury.

What is the preferred initial anticoagulant in a patient with renal impairment (CrCl 20 mL/min) and suspected PE? — LMWH at a reduced dose, monitoring anti‑Xa if available; UFH is an alternative if anti‑Xa not available.
A patient with PE has a PaO₂ of 70 mmHg and a PaCO₂ of 30 mmHg. What does this indicate? — Hypoxemia with respiratory alkalosis, typical of PE.
Why is a pleural effusion common in PE? — It is a reactive exudate due to inflammation and increased vascular permeability.

What is paradoxical embolism and which cardiac defect predisposes to it? — An embolus passes from venous to arterial system via a right‑to‑left shunt; a patent foramen ovale (PFO) or atrial septal defect (ASD) is common.

A 58‑year‑old man with massive PE is hypotensive. What is the first-line treatment? — Thrombolysis with tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) if no contraindication; otherwise consider surgical embolectomy.
Which laboratory test is used to monitor therapeutic LMWH? — Anti‑Xa activity; target 0.3–0.7 IU/mL for therapeutic range.
What is the typical threshold for a positive D‑dimer in a 70‑year‑old? — Age‑adjusted cut‑off: 70 × 0.01 = 0.7 µg/mL FEU.
Why is a low‑molecular‑weight heparin preferred over UFH in low‑resource settings? — Predictable pharmacokinetics, no need for aPTT monitoring, and lower risk of heparin‑induced thrombocytopenia.

Explain why pulmonary infarction occurs in only a minority of PE cases. — Collateral circulation and variable embolus size mean that complete occlusion of a segmental artery is required for infarction.
